speechtext: should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. speechtext: The charge to which my hon. friend has referred, which was in effect dismissed by the Ontario court of appeal, was a charge of fabricating evidence laid under section 177 of the old code. Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday last the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) asked a question regarding the Port Mann shops, and at an earlier date the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn) asked similar questions in connection with the same matter. I regret the delay in answering both of them.
The management of Canadian National Railways now advises as follows. Reduction in the personnel employed by the railway for repair and servicing of rolling stock is explained by the dieselization of motive power, the cumulative effect of improvement in design and construction, increased capacity of freight cars, improvement in repair methods and practices, and the acquisition of much new equipment. As a point for repair and servicing of locomotives and cars Port Mann has been affected by the efforts of the management to maintain a proper balance between rolling stock and repair expenses and the volume of traffic. In effecting this reduction in personnel the legitimate interest of each employee affected has been properly protected in accordance with the governing wage agreement, and discussions have been held with the representatives of the appropriate labour organizations.

Mr. Chairman, at this time I should like to make a few remarks about the postal service in Toronto-Rosedale. I think it is important to demonstrate at the outset that the representations have come to me and have been made in a community service and non-partisan spirit. The area concerned is the Yonge-Bay-Bloor district of Toronto, and the representations are those of the businessmen's association of the area.
It so happened that during the Christmas season of 1954 they held one of their regular 
luncheon meetings, and I was pleased to be a guest. The subject under discussion at this meeting was "Christmas as applied to every day of the year". The very eminent speaker was Rev. Dr. Cecil Swanson, rector of St. Paul's church, which is within the district. The guests at the head table were diversified and representative of the community. In this atmosphere the men of the community raised their postal problems. I am not asking the Acting Postmaster General to approach their problems as Santa Claus would, but rather in accordance with the spirit of the talk, in which we were asked to apply patience and prudence. The aim is that all concerned may receive satisfaction, which I know can be forthcoming.
The basic problem of the postal service in Rosedale has been one which the businessmen have approached with great patience in the past. For many years, at the intersection of St. Clair and Yonge streets, owing to the depressed conditions of the 1930's and the labour and material shortages of the wartime period, there was a shortage of space and appropriate facilities. However in due time-I must say, without any particular representations from me as the elected member-notably in the year 1949, a great improvement was made. Then during the period of the last parliament a $3 million office building was erected in that district, which provides expanded and improved postal facilities.
I emphasize that this was done by the department in its good judgment on the basis of need, after patience and restraint on the part of the community. Postal service in the immediate vicinity of that part of Yonge street is much better, and I thank the Postmaster General and particularly the deputy postmaster general for what has been done there, because it is indeed much appreciated.
I must also report that in the Yonge-Bay-Bloor area we have postal station F, which is capable of handling perhaps the largest volume of mail in the Toronto region so far as branch stations are concerned.
This is what has been going on in the last number of years. But, Mr. Chairman, this section has now become something quite different from what it was before the war. It is now the uptown crossroads of metropolitan Toronto. It is also the uptown hub of the financial offices in so far as many large corporations are concerned. In addition, as the result of much public pressure it has become a redevelopment area for mid-town apartment dwellers. Here we have a condition of expansion in mid-century, within the twentieth century; and the postal service, like everything else, has had growing pains.

Previous to the beginning of the year, let us say, merchants in great numbers were picking up their own mail, and delivery was slower than necessary. There was also a shortage of staff and space because of the great expansion that has occurred. I do believe the deputy postmaster general has dealt with the matter on a short-time basis in a very sympathetic and satisfactory way, for the present. He was very quick to see, in the light of the report on the Toronto problem, that more staff and space were necessary. These were forthcoming, and in time I believe they will produce a great improvement there in so far as postal service is concerned. We believe that given time, with the new rental space, much will be provided that will be good for all concerned. In addition there will be more letter carriers on the walks to provide better service to merchants receiving their mail.
However, I would say this; that the split premises, one permanent and the other rental premises newly acquired, are not now large enough. These split premises cannot make for the best possible service in this important shopping and business area. I do think we have to look for something better. While the businessmen concerned are restrained in their representations, I know they feel the time has come when the department should think about one consolidated building for all postal services in this area.
We all realize that it is the function of the Department of Public Works to make this consolidation and on these estimates I do not want to go into detail as to that matter. However, I would point out that Rosedale was neglected with respect to its public facilities during the 1930's because of depressed conditions. In the 1940's it was restricted because of wartime conditions and the aftermath thereof. We now think that progress toward a new building is most important in this all-important area.

do not have it in front of me, but I believe there is a section of the Civil Service Act which permits departments to impose disciplinary penalties when necessary. Mr. Chairman, I want to express my personal regret that the Postmaster General is in ill health and unable to be here in the House of Commons. I might just say that I think it might well be that the Postmaster General's ill health is partly due to the fact that he had an extremely difficult initiation as Postmaster General. Of course the result was that when he tried to pilot his estimates through the committee of supply there was a barrage of criticism from those who were opposed to such an increase in the taxation of our people. In this regard I want to extend my congratulations to the people in the Post Office Department far and wide. I come from a rural area where we have rural mail couriers. I know of no people who give finer service to the public and who show greater fidelity to their responsibilities. I think the old saying that the King's mail-now the Queen's mail-must go through is taken to heart by our rural mail couriers throughout the service. Perhaps that is a policy carried out by all those in the employ of the Post Office Department. In saying that I do not mean for one moment to say that everything in this far-flung public department is as good as it should be. I think the department should at all times try to give better service, and at the same time should try to cut any unnecessary expenditures.
There are one or two things I should like to point out. First, I am wondering whether some of the $7J million of surplus is perhaps the result of economies which mean curtailment of the service to our people. I have here the report of the Postmaster General dated March 31, 1954. I might say it is regrettable that while this report was tabled in the house on January 10, 1955, it was only today that I was able to get a copy of it. I was told the reason was that more copies were not in print, and I had to get one from the sessional papers office. That situation is rather regrettable, in view of the fact that it is for the year 1954. I think the fact that copies have not been distributed to the members of the house is an unfortunate circumstance.
This report states that in the last year- that is in 1954-there was a decrease of 57 in the number of post offices in Canada. I should like to know the reason for the closing of those post offices. Was it simply because the revenue return was so low, or was it because they were in neighbourhoods where they were no longer giving service to the people?
I do not agree with the statement by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace yesterday, when he was asking the government to discontinue the service or operations of the post office savings bank. Too often, I think, we have coming from that corner of the chamber certain suggestions with regard to economies without any indication of how they may reflect on the service to our people.
Taking the figures from the report of the Postmaster General for 1954, I see that there has been an increase in the use of this facility of the Post Office Department. As an example, for the fiscal year 1945 the balance on deposit, in round figures, was $28 million, but by 1954 it had increased to $39 million.

We in parliament receive the demands and requests of the people of Canada. It is our responsibility to give careful consideration to them, and on the basis of their merit and propriety we take action in order to meet those demands. In the case of the town of Beverly it seems to me that the requests of the people for consideration in the matter of expanded postal facilities have not been met. The story is long, but briefly it involves a fast growing community of some 4,500 people who at the present time have a little shack for a post office which has some 160 square feet of lobby space.
It is quite obvious that this is inadequate for a community with the rapid growth of Beverly, Alberta. The people there are very displeased and in some quarters quite angry.

I do say most strongly that the situation is not comparable in any way with banking institutions which handle far greater quantities of money than the post office. The record of theft in the banking institutions of Canada is not in any way comparable with the bad record of the post office.
I repeat, Mr. Chairman, this record shows, first, that adequate care and attention is not being taken of Her Majesty's mail, particularly the valuable section; and, second, that the post office is derelict in following through, once a theft has occurred, in an attempt to find out the circumstances and prosecute those responsible for it.

In this connection, I come once again to the answer given in the house this afternoon by the parliamentary assistant that it would have been easy enough to tell us how much money had been stolen from them, but that they really do not know, without a great deal of work, what was being done about those thefts, who was being prosecuted and who was not, what action was being instituted, and so forth. Some reference was made in the reply this afternoon to the post office savings bank. I wish to say first to the hon. member for Moose Mountain that there never was any suggestion on my part that the post office savings bank and its facilities should be discontinued. I did suggest ways and means of more efficiently and more cheaply accomplishing that particular function of the post office to the parliamentary assistant, who gave a reply in that connection.
It is unfortunate that the government, having spent some hundred thousand dollars for a management report and having reorganized their department very largely on the basis of that report, subsequently finds it necessary to come to this house and argue against the conclusions of that report. The report specifically said that the saving if the post office savings bank were discontinued would be $377,000. This afternoon the department comes into the house and says, "Yes, but it is only $150,000 that the savings bank is costing us". When we pay for a report and organize a department on the basis of that report we should be prepared to stand on that report if it is a good report; and if it is not, we should not be reorganizing on the basis of it.
Finally there is the question of the two-a-day mail. I have never heard a weaker explanation or set of figures-or rather, lack of figures-given than this afternoon in that connection. The parliamentary assistant came in and said, "If we follow through with the member's suggested plan we will have a lot of additional expenditure". Then he stopped -a dead stop-and went on to refer to the

fact that he-presumably his department- considered the public would not approve of this measure.
Mr. Chairman, when we come into this house and sit here month in and month out doing our sincere best to do a job for the people of Canada and when we come forward with an idea which in our estimation is a sound and sensible idea, when we suggest that it is an idea which would not result in major increases in expenditure, it disturbs us, to say the least, that the minister should feel that he can come in as the Delphic oracle and announce without giving any reasons whatsoever just that it will incur additional expenditure. I ask the parliamentary assistant if he will stand up later and give this house some definite information, at least a few figures, as to where the additional expenditure would arise in this suggested course of having two deliveries a day for five days a week instead of the present course of having one delivery a day of mail six days a week. I pay no attention whatsoever to his statement that the public would not like the new system. Those of us on this side of the house individually are certainly capable of coming to some conclusions as to what the people want; that is what the minister has done. I feel that our views on that subject are at least as good as his.

the second reading of Bill No. 406, to incorporate Stanmount Pipe Line Company.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?

Will the sponsor give an
explanation of the bill?

Yes; perhaps I should make a brief statement with regard to this bill.
It is proposed that the Stanmount Pipe Line Company be organized for the purpose of transporting petroleum from the United States and Canada through Canada back into the United States markets. The route of the proposed pipe line will be from Beaverlodge field, North Dakota through the Tioga field, North Dakota through southeastern Saskatchewan to Cromer, Manitoba.
The length of the proposed line will be approximately 140 miles and will tie in with the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company system at Cromer, Manitoba. The size of the proposed line will be 10J inches, outside diameter, and will have an ultimate capacity of approximately 40,000 barrels per day. The estimated cost of the proposed line is approximately $6 million, about half of which will be expended in Canada.
The Interprovincial Pipe Line Company have indicated they now have enough spare capacity to accommodate the through-put of oil of the proposed line and have also indicated their willingness to transport this crude in bond via their Canadian and United States -Lakehead Pipe Line-lines to the United States markets.
A thorough investigation of the oil production available from the above mentioned fields, and markets which the proposed pipe line system will serve in the United States, has been completed. These fields are located in the Williston basin which has estimated reserves of 600 million barrels of crude oil and the area will develop rapidly when additional outlets are provided. Therefore, it is expected the available markets of 30,000 barrels per day along the Interprovincial Pipe Line route in the United States will ultimately be transported through the Stanmount-Interprovincial-Lakehead system. These markets of 30,000 barrels per day in the United States are for 40 degrees to 42 degrees API crude which is presently being transported by railroad tank car and truck, a much more expensive method of transportation than by pipe line. It is to be noted that no other pipe line services this area to eastern markets. In addition, any crude developed in southeastern Saskatchewan which meets the above specifications will be afforded an immediate market.
A Delaware corporation known as the Stanmount Pipe Line Company, Inc., has been incorporated and it is proposed that it will be

Private Bills
a wholly-owned subsidiary of Stanmount Pipe Line Company. It is further proposed that this United States corporation will build and operate the section of the proposed line in the United States.
It is intended that the direction of pumping be reversible in the proposed pipe line and, in the interests of national emergency, the existence of this pipe line system will make readily available to both the Canadian and United States governments the enormous crude oil reserves of the Williston basin. By the same token, Canadian crude can be made available to the United States.
The proven and semi-proven reserves of crude oil in the producing areas to be served by the proposed pipe line and the refineries to be served by this system make available desirable markets in the United States. In the opinion of competent engineers, these known factors justify the financing of this project. Expert evidence by highly competent pipe line engineers will be available when this bill is before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, May 6, consideration of the motion of Mr. Argue for the second reading of Bill No. 304, to amend the Small Loans Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. M. Benidickson (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to continue the debate on the proposed amendment to the Small Loans Act which was introduced by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) on May 6. The debate is reported in Hansard at pages 3535 to 3542. From the point of view of the Department of Finance it is not my purpose to defend in every particular the Small Loans Act as it exists at the present time. I did, however, indicate to the house that the Small Loans Act was created upon the recommendations of the banking and commerce committees of 1937 and 1938, and received over the years a great deal of attention from former members of the house. The present

act did make some very substantial improvements at that time. It did provide for the first time some form of government regulation. It has substantially, one might probably say to all intents and purposes, eliminated the unscrupulous loan sharks who were being investigated by our committees at that time, and I think it is safe to say that since its inception it has resulted in the availability of an adequate amount of legitimate capital for the small borrower who is not able to provide the normal type of security that is traditionally required by most of our chartered banks.
It may be, Mr. Speaker, that after 15 years it would be appropriate for the house to review the advantages and merits of the present statute. I would agree with the hon. member for Assiniboia that doubtless our chief interest and attention would be directed to the desirability and merit of the existing maximum rate of charge or interest. I would agree also that the house, if it were to make a review of the act, would probably also like to concentrate on the advisability of continuing the present ceiling of $500. Only loans up to $500 come within the regulations of the act.
Hon. members will recall that as recently as last year this house, in revising the Bank Act, took a very important step that has a bearing on the small loan field. I refer to the authorization given by virtue of the Bank Act revision to the chartered banks enabling them for the first time to lend money on the security of chattel mortgages. In his speech on May 6 the hon. member for Assiniboia commended the Bank of Commerce which, notwithstanding the lack of opportunity of taking chattel mortgage security, pioneered in what might be called the small personal loan field; in other words, the making of loans where the normal type of security that is usually requested by a bank is not available. I am thinking of non-business loans where a bank normally expects that the borrower will be able to present security such as bonds, shares, insurance equities and the like. This is a field in which the small loan companies are so active.
It is a little too soon to know to what extent the chartered banks are going to increase their interest in this type of lending because the act was only amended a year ago and reports in connection with this new type of business are not yet available. However, I think it will be obvious to members of the house that if the chartered banks do take a bigger share of the lending in this field it will doubtless be the fact that they will be taking the better share, and we will
Small Loans Act
still have before us concern about who is going to serve the poorer risks.
It is the view of the Department of Finance that it would be unwise on the part of this house to accept the bill now offered by the hon. member for Assiniboia without a very extensive review by the banking and commerce committee. I think it would be reasonable to take evidence from the chartered banks as to the extent to which they have taken a more active part in this field.
I believe that we would be required to give good notice to those, who are in this field, and there are many not only as licensees but as companies. It is our feeling that this could not be handled in an efficient way this session, being introduced as it has been at this late time.
In addition to that, I should like to point out to the house that in our view there are some features of the proposed amendments which obviously would not be acceptable to most members of the house. Indeed, I question whether, when considered by the sponsor, they would be very satisfactory to him. It is not clear in the proposed bill what the hon. member for Assiniboia has in mind with reference to the licensing provision, since no amendment is suggested in his amending bill with respect to the proviso in subsection 1 of section 5. This proviso states that a licence is not required by a money lender where the cost of the loan does not exceed 12 per cent per annum, which is equivalent to -95 of 1 per cent per month. If the maximum permissible rate under the act were reduced to 1 per cent per month, the effect would be that only those lenders charging between [DOT]95 of 1 per cent and 1 per cent would be licensed.
Furthermore, under subsection 1 of section 6 as it now stands, the maximum rate of interest after the expiry of the termination of the loan is to be 12 per cent per annum. Again, as I say, that is -95 of 1 per cent per month. Clause 2 of the bill of the hon. member for Assiniboia would permit a slightly larger rate, namely 1 per cent per month. For these reasons alone, I think it would be unfortunate if this bill were proceeded with at this time.
Hon. members are probably aware that the Small Loans Act is administered by the department of insurance which reports to the Minister of Finance. This department has a very strict policy, not only for licensing but for scrutinizing the charges of these companies and the annual statements that they present. I think it is fair to those in charge of this administration to say that they have probably been carrying out the supervision in this field in a cleaner and

Small Loans Act
better way than probably any other country of which we know. The department itself is most anxious to ensure that the maximum allowable rate is set as low as possible, but it has to be consistent with the availability of funds for those people who require the loans. It is true in recent years that the expense of doing business has risen considerably. At the same time it is known by the annual report that the volume of business of this type has also increased very importantly, and volume is an important factor in their cost ratios.
These features just tend to aggravate one of the problems that seem to be inherent in this business, and that is that a rate that may be too low for a company with a small volume of loans may be too high for a company with a big volume of loans. I believe that is borne out when one looks at the last report submitted to this house under the Small Loans Act. I refer to pages 12 and 13 of the 1953 report under the Small Loans Act, where it is shown that one company dominates the field in small loans to the extent of having something over $50 million of the $71 million of loans for 1953 governed by this act. This particular company made 530,000 loans in 1953 and the average loan was $226.
Now, I just want to indicate to the house what would happen to that business if this particular bill were accepted. I find that this company, which has the advantage of volume which is admittedly a necessity for profitable operation in this field, had total charges, that is charges or interest, amounting to $12-6 million. Their expenses were $6 [DOT] 6 million, leaving a gross profit of $5-9 million. They paid income tax of $2-9 million, leaving a net profit of roughly $3 million. If the interest were cut in half as proposed-this is by no means considered to be all interest but involves the work of drawing the security documents and so on, so that charges are a very important factor-this would be the effect on the balance sheet of this company. The income would be $6-3 million, the expenses were $6 * 6 million so there would be a loss of $300,000.
Now, of course, the sponsor says that companies of this type can cut their costs. This attitude is typical of the members of that party who believe they are able to run everyone else's business a little better than the proprietor. He gives a few illustrations. He said that for one thing they should be able to cut the cost of borrowed money, I do not know these people personally, but I cannot imagine these businessmen paying any more in interest than they needed to pay. The hon. member makes a comparison with the Bank

of Commerce and says there is a spread there between the cost of money in the small loans department of the Bank of Commerce as compared with the cost of borrowed money in the personal loan company field.
I hope all members of the house will realize that would undoubtedly be the case. The Bank of Commerce or any other chartered bank gets its money from depositors who are paid a very low rate of interest. The small loan company lender must go to the banks or other sources and borrow at the normal rates. He referred to advertising costs. It is not my purpose to say that advertising costs of these small loan companies are justified, but I will remind the hon. member for Assiniboia that when he read the brief the Canadian Bank of Commerce presented to the banking and commerce committee of 1954 he should have read what the general manager of that bank told the committee respecting advertising. He said that advertising was a very important thing in this kind of business. As reported at page 822 of the banking and commerce committee report, he said.:
The present basis is not sufficient to permit the necessary publicity and development in rendering service of greatest breadth.
He was saying that the rate they were obliged to charge was so low he felt they could not afford the advertising which would bring in the volume to increase the service.
In the same report on small loan companies I find that the only other company which has a large proportion of its money out in small loans rather than loans that are not covered by the act would be in this position if this particular amendment were adopted. It reported in 1953 an income of $669,000. Its expenses were $599,000. Its gross profit was $69,000 and the profit after tax was $37,000. If you cut this income in half there would be a loss of approximately $300,000, which is just about 50 per cent of its total income.
And every other licensee, every other company reporting under the Small Loans Act, has a smaller percentage of its business under the act than outside the act. I know the hon. member for Assiniboia suggested in his speech that we should have something in the nature of a government guarantee on loans to people who have not security, in a manner such as is now followed by the government in respect of home owners and owners of farms. I am not going to argue the merits of that proposal at this stage, but it would be obvious to him, too, that an undertaking of that kind would not be entered into until a great deal more study had been made of it than has been made to date.

And so what I am pointing out now is that in asking the elimination of the source of funds for these necessitous persons who want small loans, before any other alternative is available, he is making the proposal that the source of these funds obviously would completely disappear.
I, too, have read the brief to which the hon. member for Assiniboia referred, namely that of the Bank of Commerce before the banking and commerce committee last year. While the hon. member made some quotations from the brief, I feel that his quotations were extremely convenient from his point of view. While I am not particularly taking sides, I do think that for the purpose of information of hon. members it is very desirable that some of the other side of the coin be placed on the record. The general manager of the Bank of Commerce is reported at page 809 of the proceedings of the committee on banking and commerce as having said, with respect to these personal loans:
The charge is only to a small extent to recover interest cost: by far the greater cost is in direct operating expense quite apart from the cost of funds in use.
The hon. member for Assiniboia pointed out that the average yield, since the inception of the Bank of Commerce plan, was 10-46 per cent. But he did not say that in the same brief the general manager of the bank pointed out that after paying taxes and averaging the business done since 1936 the net profit to the bank was only -77 of 1 per cent. And I think it would be obvious to most members that not a great deal of capital would be available to borrowers if the net profit was to amount to only -77 of 1 per cent.
I would also remind hon. members that while this one small loan company which, as I said, is dominant in the small loans field under the act, had all its loans and all its business within the act, the Bank of Commerce in its personal loans department did only 30 per cent of its business on loans under $500. Everyone realizes of course that it is much more expensive to deal with a great many small loans, where the number of interviews, collection work and so on is just as great, than it is to deal with a fewer number of larger loans.
Then again the hon. member for Assiniboia picked out of the report of the committee on banking and commerce the reference to the loss ratio reported by the Bank of Commerce 

the reference to bad debts. He used the figure in the brief which was that of one-tenth of 1 per cent. But he did not inform the
Small Loans Act
house that the general manager of the bank, in presenting the same brief, said:
The payment record however has been achieved during a period of very high employment. Under such conditions it would have been less than prudent not to build up an adequate reserve for the future.
He said, at the time of presenting the brief:
Our reserve is now one-quarter per cent of funds employed. Losses currently appear to be running at about this rate.
The hon. member for Assiniboia also referred to an operating profit in 1952 by the Bank of Commerce in this department of 2-48 per cent. However, he did not point out to the house that after paying taxes the profit of the Bank of Commerce in this particular personal loans department in 1952 was only 1 -24 per cent. And he, further, had available to him the 1953 results which showed that the net profit by the Bank of Commerce, after income tax, in the small loans department was 1-11 per cent.
I think most members realize that this is not a particularly attractive business profit. To some extent I believe it indicates why other chartered banks, which the hon. member for Assiniboia was scolding for not entering the field, have been rather sceptical about it, particularly prior to the time the house authorized them to take security under chattel mortgages.
I reiterate that in my view the bill itself would not even carry out completely the desires of its sponsor, particularly in connection with the clauses overlooked that have reference to regulations. I do feel that while the house may very profitably look into a matter of this kind at the next session, through one of its committees, the remaining period of this session is not such that we could do an adequate and efficient job of-getting the proper amount of evidence before a bill of this kind could be accepted.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few moments to do a bit of thinking out loud in connection with this bill. I am not sure one can throw much more light on the principle we are discussing, but I would like to say at the beginning that even though the bill has deficiencies-and I admit there are deficiencies in it-it is still worthy of discussion; and I believe that out of this discussion there is likely to come some crystallization of views with respect to this whole business of small loans. For this reason I congratulate the hon. member for Assiniboia upon his enterprise in introducing the bill. If it does nothing more than point up the need for some institution to make small loans to people whose

Small Loans Act
credit has not yet been established, or who are not considered creditworthy, it will have served a useful purpose.
After the bill was introduced I took the trouble to look back over the record in Hansard of the discussion that took place when the Small Loans Act was passed. I recall particularly the content of the speeches of Mr. Ilsley and the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) who spoke at some length at that time. I took note of the difficulties which it was thought they faced in that day in attempting to set a ceiling limit on interest rates under circumstances that might possibly dry up the source of funds and drive people into the clutches of the small loan sharks.
I think perhaps many of the fears expressed at that time were well founded. Evidently it was the experience of people in other countries that at any time they did attempt to set ceilings that were too low on these small loans, it did have the effect of drying up the source. There is no question about that. But even so, it does seem shocking in this day and age of comparatively easy money that people should have to pay 26 per cent and upwards a year for their borrowings. The present act does provide a ceiling limit of 26 per cent. It is supposed to be 2 per cent a month, but, as the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) said when he spoke on the original bill, it does amount to something over 26 per cent yearly. As I say, it does seem shocking. That to me is usurious, if it is not usury. I do not know where the line is to be drawn between an ordinary rate of interest that is legitimate and usury; but certainly a rate of 26 per cent a year is usurious and indicates not only characteristics of leeches but I would go further and say bloodsuckers. I am afraid there are too many bloodsuckers who are anxious to live on the avails of destitution. That is exactly what it is. These people are prepared to take advantage of the fact that other people are often forced to come to them for accommodation, for small loans, that they simply cannot do without. To take advantage of them, it seems to me, is certainly invoking the wrath of the ancient prophets who said that these people grinding down the faces of the poor are the worst leeches known to society.
Well, as I say, it is still unfortunate and shocking that in this day such a thing should be. But I will say this. My reading and my experience have both proven that as soon as the Small Loans Act was passed it eliminated to a very large degree the leech or the bloodsucker. We are not plagued with such, as they are in some other countries. While I was in British East Africa last summer, it

was drawn to my attention that the rates of interest charged not only on small loans but on medium loans of medium length and on long-term loans were shockingly high, in some cases 50 per cent to 60 per cent, and that the rate on the ordinary commercial loan was something that we would not countenance in this country. They told me that the loan sharks thrived over there with no regulation whatsoever. Therefore, I do say that the Small Loans Act has done a pretty good job.
I am afraid I must agree with the parliamentary assistant to the minister who said that we have to be careful not to put a limitation on the rate of interest that would drive the funds out of the field and make it impossible for people to get accommodation. I am inclined to believe that this bill is putting the cart before the horse. I do agree with the parliamentary assistant that as soon as it is convenient this whole matter should be studied by a committee. It should be given the broadest and the deepest possible study, with a view to finding some solution to the whole problem.
I said that to pass this bill now might be putting the cart before the horse. The reason I say that is this. We should direct our efforts towards finding sources of funds that may be lent at smaller rates of interest than 2 per cent a month. Before we set a limit to the small loans that are now being made- that is, a limit smaller than the present one- we should investigate every possible means of extending and strengthening the credit union system. In my judgment, that is one of the finest measures for eliminating the sort of usurious charges that we have known in the past and about which we are now complaining.
Some of the provinces in the dominion are doing a good job in encouraging the development of the credit union organizations plan. It is an excellent thing. In this house we should give consideration to ways by which the dominion parliament and government can assist in extending and strengthening the credit union set-up. The second thing we should be considering is ways and means of extending the kind of thing which the Bank of Commerce has been doing for some years, and rather successfully. What they have done has shown what other banks could do efficiently and well.
I congratulate the Canadian Bank of Commerce on their personal loans division. While I am doing so, I should like to correct one thing which the parliamentary assistant said, perhaps inadvertently, in comparing the cost of the funds which are available for loan by the Canadian Bank of Commerce small loans

division on the one hand, and the small loans companies on the other hand. I think the parliamentary assistant did say that the cost of the funds obtained from the depositors of the Canadian Bank of Commerce would be much smaller than that borne by the small loans corporations. Well, the fact is, of course, that the Canadian Bank of Commerce does not lend the depositors' money through its small loans division. What it does is to create the loans at the moment they are made. All it needs to have is the cash reserve required now at a percentage of approximately 8 per cent, as required by the Bank of Canada. Naturally, their costs are much lower. I can understand what the hon. member has said, and the force of his argument. As a matter of fact, what I have just now brought before the house does strengthen the argument.
The cost of the funds of the Canadian Bank of Commerce small loans section is very much less than the cost of the funds that are lent by the small loans companies. My own feeling is that other banks could enter this field and by so doing could give a real public service. It might be possible to induce them to get into the field. If so, it would help to solve the problem to some extent, although there would be a group of needy individuals who yet would not be served. They will have to be the responsibility of some other institution or organization. My own judgment is that we may have to set up some institution in our land, maybe provincially or nationally, backed by the government, but not necessarily a government institution. I do not think it would be wise for a government institution to attempt it, but some institution backed by the government, an institution designed perhaps to consolidate the small debts of the people who have met with adversity and are really in need of credit, but whose needs are yet so small that they would not be an attraction to the ordinary lending institutions to bother with them. Perhaps I should include people who have not proved themselves to be creditworthy.
I am satisfied that such an institution would require government backing. I am also satisfied that in the long run it would lose money. But, Mr. Speaker, I point out that it would be cheaper in the long run to assist people through an institution of that kind than it would be to pick up the dregs after they have been forced into doing things because they cannot get a bit of credit.
There are thousands of people in our country who need a little money and who oftentimes need it quickly because of tragedy that has struck their families. Perhaps they have no place to go for it except to their friends. If they are not living with their
Small Loans Act
friends who have the wherewithal, what are they going to do? I am sure they would do everything they are capable of doing to manage their affairs successfully, but some people are just not built so that they can manage. Such people are managed and their affairs are managed for them by institutions. It looks to me as though it would be worth while thinking about some institution, government-backed, to help these people when they are in need with a small loan that may not be worth bothering about by some of these other institutions.
If we could get those three things working, it seems to me we might perhaps be able to put a limit of 1 per cent a month on these small loans without causing distress among people who have to go to the small loans companies to get their credit. I would agree with the parliamentary assistant to the minister that we should give this matter a most thorough and earnest study and bring it before a committee perhaps at the next session to see if it would be possible to work out provisions for meeting the needs of those people who have no credit standing but who are nevertheless human beings and ought to be taken care of, and not neglected. Otherwise it does not seem as if we are doing our duty to human beings. I congratulate the mover of this motion on the bill. I think his bill will serve a very useful purpose, although in its present form I am not sure it will do the job it is designed to do.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in my place to support the bill that is now before us. I was one of the lucky ones who in my high school days attended a separate school and had to make a rather thorough study of church history. While studying church history I was informed that for hundreds of years-as a matter of fact, for more years than was not the case -the teachings of the Christian church were that the charging of interest was something to be considered unethical. For many long centuries Christians were not allowed to charge any interest whatsoever.
I only regret that because of the members on the government side who were on last year's banking and commerce committee the introduction of a bill of this sort is at all necessary. I understand that the banks of Canada at that time expressed their willingness to enter the personal loans field if they would be permitted to charge, not 6 per cent as they are now permitted, but 12 per cent per annum on personal loans. However, some of those so-called monetary reformers who were on the committee raised their hands in holy horror at the idea of allowing the chartered banks to raise interest rates

Supply-Post Office
from 6 per cent to 12 per cent, and they were not allowed to do so. I regret that this happened because I feel that, if our chartered banks had been given authority to enter the personal loans field and to charge 1 per cent per month on loans which were secured by means of chattel mortgages, all major Canadian finance companies today would have disappeared and we would not have had to consider a bill of this sort.
The next matter I should like to raise is the question of whose money is being used by the finance companies of Canada. There was something to be said for a man when he decided to risk his own money and also being able to decide how much compensation he ought to have before he would decide to take the risk. However, that argument can no longer be applied to the finance companies in their operations at the present time. From all the information I have, finance companies obtain the vast bulk of their money from the life insurance companies and from the chartered banks of Canada. They pay in the neighbourhood of 4| per cent for this money. They use this money and charge 24 per cent for the use of it. According to my calculations that represents a charge for the cost of handling of 19J per cent. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) has placed enough evidence on the record to indicate that these finance companies, if they wished, would be able to operate at a much lower rate. If they were not able to operate, I do not think we who are supposed to represent the interests of the Canadian people at large should be unduly worried. I was the one who interrupted the parliamentary assistant, and I said we would like to see the finance companies out of business. We would be doing a real service to the people of Canada if legislation were so framed that they would be unable to continue operations, at least on the basis of charging 2 per cent per month.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

Before the resolution carries there are one or two comments I should like to make on perhaps a different plane from that on which we were dealing with matters at five o'clock. The hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace was more or less in the sordid realm of criminal procedure as it affected the department. I should like to take the minds of the committee for a moment away from that mundane subject to the more aesthetic and artistic one of the administration of the department in so far as its choice of stamps is concerned. I am sure it will be a welcome relief to the Acting Postmaster General to get translated to that realm even for a moment.
I was a stamp collector at a very early age.

I am glad to hear that because some of the things I have to say will be things which have been told to me by stamp collectors. The Acting Postmaster General perhaps can tell me as a philatelist; I am not quite sure about the pronunciation but as long as we both agree that neither one of us is quite sure I shall not be called to order for mispronouncing it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is spelled the same way in Hansard.

Seriously, I think there is
something that should be said to this committee with respect to this matter. We have had various series of stamps during the last few years. We have the fur-bearing series which has had animals depicted on the stamps of this country. On one of them I noticed an Indian or trapper of some kind nailing a beaver hide, I think it was, to a log cabin, but that beaver skin was much larger than the trapper himself. Then we have another one, which possibly might have some significance to the married men of this country, where I noticed an Indian warrior or an Indian buck squatting back of his tepee while the squaw is doing the work of nailing a deer skin to the front of the tepee. I am sure that is something which we all would hope to emulate but I am not so sure how practical it would be.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And how!

"And how" is right. Now we have the wildlife series on which I am not going to make any extensive comments. I just wonder why we have these various

series of stamps in view of the omissions I think have been made by this department. I have some of the wildlife series in front of me. I am not going to elaborate on them for the moment or to elaborate on them at all. But certainly if anyone looks at the 4-cent stamp he will see what I mean. I hope that some time during the evening the Acting Postmaster General or his parliamentary assistant will satisfactorily define for the committee just what is depicted on that 4-cent stamp. I thought it was a muskox. Certainly it has that lonely and rather sinister and ferocious glare that you would associate with the muskox.
Perhaps the minister of northern affairs could tell you that.

I looked at the report of the Postmaster General this afternoon and I saw that in 1954 what was depicted on the 4-cent stamp was a mountain goat. But when I look at the stamp and the one reproduced in the report I cannot tell except that I think the mountain goat looks possibly more intelligent than the muskox. Then I had a note later on in the afternoon from a friend of ours in the press gallery who suggested that someone should comment on the fact that this 4-cent stamp had depicted on it a judge of the supreme court with a wig on. I think that is perhaps a reflection on the judges of the court, but nevertheless it suggests the difficulty in deciding just what is depicted on these stamps. When you cannot tell the difference between a muskox, a mountain goat and a judge of the supreme court, I would suggest that there is something slightly wrong or something askew with the engraving which is being carried on by the department at the moment. I noticed the reply of the acting minister this afternoon to the hon. member for St. Paul's, I think it was, wherein he said that the contract has been let for three years to the Canadian Bank Note Company Limited and will come up for renewal next year. I hope one suggestion made will be that the lithography should be improved there.
I may say that I have an editorial here. I know that one should not quote from editorials and I will not purport to quote from any editorials published in the newspapers of this country. But this is one which I know the parliamentary assistant knows quite well. It is a little paper whose publisher boasts of the fact that he spells his name with both a small "1" and a large "L". I refer to the Berwick Register. He is commenting on this 4-cent stamp and he says something to the effect that it becomes an adventure in speculation to see the reason for picturing the
Supply-Post Office
muskox on Canada's 4-cent stamps. Then he goes on to say that the muskox is a lonely creature, that he lives away up in the north and wants to be left alone; and why anyone should ever depict his countenance on this stamp and depict it in the way in which it is caricatured is something no one could understand. I do not want to go into prenatal influences or anything of that kind, but I will say this, that if any one of the mothers of this country had to lick many of these stamps, I hate to think what the effect might be upon unborn generations with this ferocious glare which one sees in these stamps.
A year ago we were criticizing the department for the stamps as far as Her Majesty was concerned. I can understand how difficult it was properly to portray her. I think it would be impossible for anyone to catch the radiant beauty, the charm, the character and the quality of Her Majesty and portray those qualities on a postage stamp. That would be an impossibility. I do not criticize the department particularly with regard to that matter but, in all seriousness, I say with regard to this series of stamps on which these animals are now being portrayed, I wonder in the first place why we find this being done. I suggest both to the parliamentary assistant and to the acting minister, both of whom were teachers before they entered the political realm, that the atlases and the nature books of this country can portray more artistically, more effectively and more beautifully the natural life of Canada than it can ever be portrayed on a postage stamp. You have a beaver which is so large that, when you look at it, you are not quite sure whether it is a mountain lion or a beaver. You have an Eskimo paddling a canoe which looks like a toothpick, and the whole situation of trying to depict the natural life of this country on postage stamps is, I suggest, something which is ineffective. I should like to know just what the explanation is. The minister may say, "We wanted to give publicity to the wildlife of this country". The minister of northern affairs issued a booklet not too long ago in which there were beautiful reproductions of the wildlife of this country. They are much more effective than any which can be put on a postage stamp. When Canadian editorial writers refer to this stamp as one which is discreditable to Canada and offensive to the artistic sense of Canadians, I suggest that the department should reconsider this whole matter of trying to depict the wildlife or the natural life of this country on postage stamps.
There is a particular reason why I raise this matter at this time. One can be sarcastic and one can poke fun at these stamps, and I think one should do so because there is a justifiable criticism. I am told by philatelists

Supply-Post Office
that the value of Canadian stamps has depreciated tremendously during the past two or three years because of the quality of reproduction we have had. There was a time not so many years ago-and the parliamentary assistant certainly remembers it and will be proud of it-when one of our Canadian stamps depicted the schooner Bluenose, a name which was remembered the other day in another connection. That was recognized throughout the philatelic world as one of the most beautiful reproductions that had ever been made. I am suggesting that in the quality of the work that is done today we are a long way removed from the quality of work which was done by the department at that time. This is a reflection on the artistic sense and the artistry and the professional skill of the engraver and the lithographer which I am sure is available to the department if they would make the proper inquiries concerning it.
I want to move from that to the matter which really motivates me in making this criticism. I am not interested in making criticism simply for the sake of criticizing, but I do wish to suggest that the department has been remiss in centring its activities on features such as that and missing the boat on other matters which should have been dealt with by the department. A year ago I raised this matter with the Postmaster General, and may I say here, as others have said, how sorry I am he is not with us and how much I hope that before too long he will be fully restored to health and back in this chamber. I discussed this matter with him at that time and we had rather extensive correspondence afterwards.
The Postmaster General was good enough to write me and to say that I had roused his interest in the historical life of the country to such an extent that he was authorizing the issue of a series of historical postage stamps which will come out some time in the future. I suggest to the Acting Postmaster General that more consideration should have been given to the matter of history prior to this. I can think of three particular events that in my opinion should have been recognized by the Post Office Department this year. It would have been much better to recognize them than to try to reproduce an Indian squaw nailing a deer hide to a frame while her husband sits smoking a pipe watching her do it. That may have some interest for tourists but I doubt it.
In Canada this year we are celebrating the 350th anniversary of the first settlement of white men north of the gulf of Mexico. It happened not in the United States but here in Canada, and happened in my own province and constituency. As a matter of fact the
[Mr. Nowlan.l
Postmaster General promised me he would issue a stamp commemorating that event but he said that after all they had these others in process and it would be two years before we could have the stamp I suggested available for distribution. We are celebrating the 350th anniversary in 1955 and although it will be a welcome tribute, shall we say, to see this stamp in 1957 it would certainly have been a lot better to have it in 1955. If you are going to continue the frankly and crudely cheap quality of the reproductions we see in our stamps today I still think it would not be too difficult to have a stamp issued between now and the end of 1955 to commemorate that event.
We are also celebrating the 200th anniversary of the return of the Acadians to the maritime provinces and the commemoration of their expulsion which occurred in 1755. Then there is another event which I would have thought would be of particular interest to the Post Office Department. I know it was brought to their attention by the Nova Scotia historical society. This is the 200th anniversary of the establishment of the first post office in Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The 100th of the first one in western Canada.

Well, 100 years from now we will celebrate the one in western Canada. But I would have thought the Post Office Department would have commemorated properly the 200th anniversary of the establishment of its own department, shall we say, because I have here extracts which appeared in the Boston Evening Post of April 28, 1755, announcing the fact that there was a post office in Halifax and that mails could be exchanged and circulated between Halifax and Boston. Many years ago the historic sites and monuments board, which comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, erected a plaque in Halifax commemorating the fact that the first post office was established in that city in 1755. As a matter of fact, the notice says, and it is of historic interest, that you will find the post office in "the first house without the south gate". You have to go out the gate and there is the house.
There are three events which I suggest, without any captious emphasis, should have been commemorated this year by a series of historical stamps. Although the Postmaster General is not here now-and we hope he will be back soon-he has said he is interested in this matter and I know there are others listening to me who are active in the administration of the department. I should

like to say to them in all kindness that I think we in this country are perhaps overlooking these matters of spiritual and cultural value and have been putting the emphasis on such things as the fur trade or wildlife, which may have a dollar and cents value. It may be a part of this materialistic concept on which I think we sometimes put too much emphasis. Perhaps it is because I come from an area where our roots are established-
In wildlife.

We have our share of wildlife, too. Perhaps it is because I come from there and appreciate the value of history that I resent the way in which this country apparently is deliberately overlooking these matters which I think should be conserved and built up if a tradition of Canada and Cana-dianism is to be established as all members of parliament want to see it established. I will not labour the matter further, but I do urge upon the Acting Postmaster General that he review this matter and see if something cannot be done this year to commemorate these events to which I have referred. I also urge upon the administration of the department that in the future more attention be paid to our history. We have the historic sites and monuments board which the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources has reorganized and incorporated and which we hope will be a more effective force in the country than ever before. I believe it should be, and I think there should be the closest co-operation between the Post Office Department and the board so that national events such as the three I have enumerated, all of which, I suggest, are of national significance, will be properly remembered by the department in the issuing of commemorative stamps.

Mr. Chairman, I think I have to assert my rights over the parliamentary assistant in this case for a reason that will appear in a moment. First of all, perhaps I should tell the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings that I am advised that the animal he mistook for a muskox was really the Acting Postmaster General listening to the speech of the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace. I must say that the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has touched me in a very sentimental spot. The only profession I have is as a historian, and I am very much interested in the commemoration of these historic events. I think one of the best ways to do so is with postage stamps which everybody can see. I am not quite sure what little influence I may have
Supply-Post Office
in the Post Office Department from time to time, but whatever influence I have there, if I ever have another chance to have any such influence, and whatever little influence I may have in the government will always be directed in that direction.
In my proper ministerial capacity I was also very pleased to be told by the new director of the national gallery only this week that for the first time, so far as he knew, the national gallery was now being consulted by the Post Office Department about the designs for their stamps. I think that is a move in the right direction.
It is.

1 also think the hon. member's suggestion about close consultation with the historic sites and monuments board is an excellent idea. But the reason I rose instead of letting the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare rise was that I felt it was essential to disagree with the perversion of history that we had from Nova Scotia. Of course I know Nova Scotians will go on claiming that the first white settlement in North America north of the gulf of Mexico was at Port Royal, but we who are connected with Newfoundland know that when Humphrey Gilbert came there in 1583 there was already a settlement there and there has been one ever since.
I should have said a permanent settlement.
When is the stamp to be issued celebrating the golden jubilee of the two western provinces, Alberta and Saskatchewan? Have arrangements been made, and when may we expect to see the stamps?
I understand arrangements have been made in that connection-

Probably in the historic
series.
-and I believe it will be about the time of the anniversary.

I am not as concerned with what is on the stamp as with the opportunity to use the stamp. I wonder if the Acting Postmaster General could say a word concerning the status of postal accommodation at air force bases. I want to apologize for delaying the committee by raising a matter of concern in my own riding, but I am sure similar situations must exist in many centres across the country.
Let me briefly outline the problem. The Department of National Defence has developed a very excellent air station at North

Supply-Post Office
Bay involving a capital cost of several millions of dollars. Everything has been provided there in a splendid fashion. There are churches, a school, a recreational hall, theatre, grocery store and all of the services that are normally required. When they were providing these things they also made provision for excellent postal accommodation. This is a real community that has developed at that base. It is on behalf of the people living in married quarters there that I should like to say a word.
This excellent accommodation has been provided, but that is as far as it has gone. The Department of National Defence requested the Post Office Department to appoint a postmaster there. The Post Office Department refused, at least that is my information, to make such an appointment unless the facilities would be made available to the general public. The Department of National Defence naturally, and quite properly, resist making their facilities available to the general public. I believe this problem, arising between two departments of government, should be worked out.
In the meantime, the people living in the married quarters, and the single quarters as well, of course, are without the usual postal services such as being able to buy money orders, stamps, the facilities of the savings bank, registered mail, etc. These people must travel three or four miles into North Bay or Gateway post office, to get these services that all of us have a right to expect these days. I am aware of the role of the armed forces postal service, but it seems to me this matter should be reviewed by both the post office and national defence departments with a view to establishing regular civilian postal facilities for the people of this important, and I might say completely modern, establishment.

The matter I have to raise tonight is a relatively minor, parochial matter compared to some of the issues the Post Office Department has been confronted with during these two days of discussion. I am genuinely sorry the minister is not able to be with us because I have been pursuing this subject with him now for two years. I believe he has been giving some serious attention to the problem, at least that was the impression I received during the discussion a year ago when we were considering these estimates.
The matter relates to the tendency for rural route deliveries in the prairie regions to decline. It affects my own constituency because from time to time a decision has to be made by the department to discontinue some of the rural routes that have been

established over a considerable number of years. In each case, the explanation given is that in this day of the universal use of the automobile farm patrons tend to go to the local post office to pick up their own mail rather than depend upon the traditional rural route delivery service. I fully appreciate that situation. The other main difficulty seems to arise from the impassable nature of certain rural roads in the western rural section.
I would point out again, Mr. Chairman, as I pointed out when we were considering this problem before, the roads in the western rural areas have always been of a somewhat indifferent nature so that problem is not one that has arisen in the recent past. There are still a large number of farm patrons living in isolated areas who do not have an automobile and are not able to handle the delivery of their own mail. I raise the issue I suppose because I still receive complaints from my constituency about the matter. In one area in particular, the town of Reston, three rural routes have been discontinued. I have received a communication that indicates that during the past winter some of the farm patrons have had to wait up to three weeks for mail delivery. The answer given by the minister last year, as recorded at page 4763 of Hansard for May 14, 1954, followed my question as to what was done in regard to the discontinuance of these rural routes and the possible solutions the department may have in mind to facilitate the delivery of mail to these relatively isolated locations. At that time the minister replied:
I am sorry but I have not that information, available at the moment because some of these routes have been readjusted. But I will be glad to look into this matter and if I have not the time to tell him before the end of the discussion on the estimates I will give him this information personally.
Unfortunately, I did not receive that information so I am repeating the question again this year. Just what are the trends in. so far as the discontinuation of these rural routes in the prairie regions is concerned? Has the trend continued during the past year and what solution, if any, is there for providing better mail deliveries to these isolated areas? Admittedly conditions in these districts are comparatively difficult. This is one of the reasons for the continuing exodus of the farmer from rural districts to the urban communities. This trend is particularly marked amongst the younger farm generation. If we are forced to discontinue postal services, that will only aggravate the problem of the de-population of our rural areas.
Closely related to this is another problem about which I should like to seek some information. This problem applies to the

house to house delivery in the rapidly growing suburban areas. It is a matter that comes to my attention from time to time, and invariably there seems to be some considerable delay before it is possible to provide house to house delivery in these rapidly growing areas around some of our expanding western communities. Then again we have certain areas in the west, particularly in the oil centres, where boom conditions prevail and where we have had a 100 per cent increase in population within the comparatively short time of three years. In one question that has come to my attention it has been pointed out that it is difficult to get the department to act by way of providing increased staff. If I mention the instance I have in mind I am sure the department will be aware of the problem, because it was a live issue around Christmastime last year. I refer of course to the town of Virden, Manitoba, which is the oil centre of our province. There was quite a furore over the lack of adequate staffing in that post office, which had resulted from the growth of population in the community in a short time to the extent of two or three thousand people. It may be, of course, that this was just a tempest in a teapot. However, I would ask just how quickly the department acts in meeting the difficulties presented to the postal service because of rapidly growing populations.
One final question. In the city of Brandon we have been waiting since 1951 for an extension to our post office. The matter has been under consideration for the past three or four years. I understand a promise was given, and I am wondering just how close to realization is the possibility of having very badly needed extended facilities in the Brandon post office.
Those are the only questions I have in mind. As I have said, perhaps they are parochial, but I would appreciate some information on these points.

think the only answer I can give is that no doubt some will be discontinued, and that there will be many new ones. Again it will depend on the individual situation, but if the hon. member has a specific case in mind I would be glad to look into it.

speechtext: In line with the exchange of discussion a while ago with respect to stamps, may I ask the parliamentary assistant if the department has prepared a stamp bearing the picture of the whooping crane, a migratory bird, which has become almost extinct. understand that a stamp depicting the whooping crane has been issued, and no doubt it was done as a result of the representations made by people who are as interested in the subject as the hon. member who has spoken.

Mr. Chairman, in the old days when we went to a burlesque show we would hear the song, I Wonder What's The Matter With the Mail; It Never Was So Late Before. I do not suggest that this is a burlesque show. I do not wish to say that this is the general song which is being sung by my constituents in this day and age. Nevertheless, it is a song that some of them must sing, and on their behalf I should like to say a word tonight. One group is rather recent, and I drew it to the attention of the department yesterday. The other group, however, consists chiefly of the residents in and around the suburbs of the hub of Nova Scotia, namely Truro. They have been singing this song for more than a year. In fact, they have been singing it ever since the new regulations went into effect a year ago last April. A few years ago these people received two mails a day. Then they got one mail delivery a day, which was not too bad. Then they were asked to pay another cent for postage, and instead of getting an improved mail service or a service which was at least as good as they were receiving before, they are getting their mail much later in the day.
I should like to say right here that the fault does not lie with the local postal authorities. We know they have gone as far as they can, and they have done everything possible having regard to the regulations

under which they must work. The problem rests right here in Ottawa, and with the Acting Postmaster General, his assistant and his departmental officials. To give our people as good a mail service as they had, to which they are entitled, the department must give them a little larger staff. On behalf of my constituents I make that plea.

There are two or three questions which remain to be cleared up. I would say in answer to the parliamentary assistant's observations tonight that all these forms to which I had reference should be filed by February 28; if not, the government assesses a penalty on the business firms not doing so. I can only hope that one department of the government is not collecting any penalty from another department in this particular case. I also hope that the same excuse which he gave to the committee, namely, that they did not have the opportunity to make it ready, will be acceptable to the Department of National Revenue with respect to all the other business firms across Canada if they choose to file between the middle and end of March.
Having said that, I should like to take the questions which I have asked to which answers have not been forthcoming and deal with them one at a time. I hope the Acting Postmaster General will not get mental indigestion by my so doing, which seems to trouble him at times. First of all, will he give us an explanation of the increase in travelling expenses in his department which have approximately tripled? They have risen from $35,000 to $100,000.

speechtext:

Supply-Post Office
I say this. In previous years the items carried over did not approximate $700,000.

While the minister and his assistant are looking for the paper, perhaps I could receive more detail on the point which was raised this afternoon regarding thefts from the post office. It would be helpful to the committee if the parliamentary assistant could point out what effort is being made to improve this situation so that four out of five people who steal from the post office will not get away free.

I think I can answer this question. This return shows every theft that has been made from the post office so far as they have been discovered. As every hon. member who has any experience in these matters knows, sometimes, especially where the thefts are committed by an employee of any organization, these thefts may go on for quite some time before they are discovered. Sometimes they are not discovered at all. Sometimes people who are responsible for these thefts are never discovered, especially when the thieves are people who break in and steal. I know this from personal knowledge because when I was a small boy my father was a postmaster and almost the last day before his resignation was accepted so that he could go to the first war the post office was robbed of quite a considerable amount of money, every cent of which he had to make up.

Did they catch the
thief?

Never; no trace was ever discovered of him. This happens quite frequently in thefts from the post office, as in other thefts in the country. The Post Office Department does exactly the same sort of thing as any other prudent organization does. It takes the best precautions it can to prevent such thefts. When any thefts are discovered, the police are informed at once and given any information that will assist them in finding the thieves. Whenever the thieves or suspects are found who can be charged, where there is enough evidence to warrant a prosecution, the department of government which has the responsibility is asked to prosecute. Of course, prosecutions for theft are carried on by the appropriate authorities which have the responsibility. I can assure the hon. member that the Post Office Department does not want to have money stolen from the post offices, that we do not encourage this practice and that we do everything we reasonably know how to discourage it. As far as the prosecutions are concerned, the Postmaster General's report for the year ending March 31, 1954, at page
