We do so by calling together, as every hon. member knows, in the first week of December, in Ottawa each and every year representatives of the 10 provincial departments, the federation of agriculture, the farmers' union, the representatives of the countries with which we trade, and the press of Canada. At this meeting full information is given as to production of and markets for all farm products. This has been going on now for 16 years, and the results, if I may say so, have been rather marvellous.
The provinces co-operate with the federal officials in making available the latest information. The federal officials pass it on to the farm organizations. The effects of it are discussed fully by all; that is, all those who are present at the conference, before the press. The press and farm organizations co-operate in passing the information on to the farmers who become as well informed as to what can be marketed as any farmers anywhere in the world.
The result has been that the farmers for many years now have kept their production of perishable products, including meats, at levels which can be marketed and have stored their surplus in the form of grain, principally wheat, which is the nearest approach to non-perishable food which exists.
When we have been threatened by disease, either of our livestock or of other products, the Department of Agriculture has grappled with the disease. Two outstanding examples are our battle against foot-and-mouth disease and rust. Every expert in every country in the world agrees that we accomplished the most complete and most expeditious eradication of foot-and-mouth disease in 1952 ever brought about in any country. This saved the livestock producers millions of dollars and price control during the period permitted production and marketing to go on at a profit.
We had 18 years without rust, but a few years ago it became known that a new race of rust to which our wheat is not resistant was on its way north. The department at once entered upon the breeding of new wheat. We did not have sufficient wheat last year which was resistant to 15B rust, but we did have Selkirk developed and distributed over the entire area. It proved itself resistant to 15B over the entire area. We have retained the 3 million bushels produced in 1954 in

this country to be seeded in 1955, and if we have a reasonably good crop we should have sufficient to seed the spring wheat area in 1956.
By these and other methods we have assisted farmers to produce the greatest quantities of the staple foods, meat, dairy and cereal products ever produced in this country. The farmers produced 7 million tons more food per year for the last three years for which we have complete figures than for each of the last three years of war which was our greatest production up to that time.
Some years ago it was realized that the piling up of surpluses resulted in reduced prices and often in reduced earnings to farmers. This was particularly true if the quality was not high. Grading systems were established in co-operation with the provinces to maintain a high standard. Even though great care has been taken to maintain high standards in the home market, it was realized that this department should cooperate with the Department of Trade and Commerce to maintain as high standards on products shipped abroad. Legislation to improve these efforts is before the house now. This is only a part of our effort to improve our markets.
We realize that for all our products excepting wheat the home market is our best market. Immigration and an increasing birth rate have increased our population. Family allowances, old age pensions and increased employment and wages have increased purchasing power. Both have improved our home markets. Price support put on by this government has stabilized and maintained returns to farmers. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture made a submission to the government regarding these matters on March 3, 1955.
It is suggested in the submission that the world has changed from being a place of scarcity of food to being a place of surpluses, most of which are held in North America.
The farmers of Canada, therefore, have very wisely managed, with the help of the December conference, to have practically all of their surpluses in the form of hard spring high protein content wheat.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture statement points out that prices of farm products have fallen further in North America than in other countries of the world. This is quite true, but prices in general after the drop are higher in North America than in other countries of the world, all of which indicates that since the war farmers in North America have had the highest prices in the world.

After making these introductory comments, the brief calls attention to two matters which are of outstanding interest to the farmers. The first is the condition of the dairy industry and the second, support prices.
The brief states that the introduction of butter substitutes, the importation of butter into Canada, the importation of cheese from New Zealand, the shrinking of world export markets for dairy foods, and other influences, have resulted in dairy producers across Canada suffering substantial economic loss.
I am inclined to agree that the importation of butter and cheese into Canada would tend to lower the returns to the producer and the net farm income is lower in the last 3 years than in 1951, but I would point out it is higher than any year from 1947 back. The shrinkage of foreign markets, however, came about partly because there has been a higher price level here than elsewhere. To have been compelled to sell in foreign markets could, therefore, have resulted in lower income. Nevertheless, the dairy industry does require support during these unsettled times.
Four recommendations are made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. The first is that there be no further importations of cheddar cheese into Canada. We have already told New Zealand, as has already been stated in this house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that there is little if any room for outside cheddar cheese in Canada. We think, however, that the highest price which can be obtained anywhere for Canadian cheddar cheese can be obtained on the Canadian market if production remains at the level of the past three years. Experience shows that all the cheese which is presently being made in Canada could be sold in Canada at Canadian prices.
The second proposal by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is that the present butter support price of 58 cents per pound be continued. That has been done. The plan followed by the prices board for the past six years of stabilizing the price on a basis of 58 cents to the producer relieves others of any risk. It makes possible a reasonable return to those who have the facilities with which to produce, and relieves the trade of any risks if they do not wish to carry butter themselves, from the summer to winter, and stabilizes the price to the consumer in winter.
The 58-cent support price on butter is the basis of the means by which the government undertakes to stabilize the dairy industry. The guarantee of the initial payment on cheese and the purchase of processed milk products on two occasions have helped. It is, therefore, somewhat disconcerting when critics greet the continuation of the support 50433-2601
Supply-Agriculture
with the inference that the taxpayer is paying for this help to the farmer. It has cost the taxpayer as such less than one-fifth of a cent per pound over the past six years to stabilize the price and practically all of that was because we cut the support down to 53 cents one year out of six. The 58 cents is paid by the consumer and he in turn has his wholesale and retail price stabilized throughout the winter.
The third proposal made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is that small surpluses be exported. We have made one small sale of butter and are investigating the possibilities of others.
The fourth proposal by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is increased protection through increased tariffs. We have not increased the tariff on imports of dairy products.
Butter is only one of the farm products upon which there is support. The federation says there should be continuous support on wheat, oats, barley, corn, hogs, eggs, cheese, butter and concentrated milk products. There is support on all but corn and concentrated milk products, and even on concentrated milk there has been assistance, in that we have on two occasions purchased concentrated milk products in order to remove surpluses from the market for the time being.
The grain supports are put on by the wheat board and freight assistance on feed grain by the Department of Agriculture. The cheese guarantee is put on under the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act. The egg, hog and butter supports are provided under the terms of the Agricultural Prices Support Act.
The federation specialized on price support in their discussions at Edmonton last winter and in the submission on March 3. We thank them for their expressions of appreciation to us for what has been accomplished to date and have followed carefully their efforts to simplify the plan of price support by a formula. I have some doubt as to whether an algebraic formula is simple to the average farmer. I believe the simple words contained in our act:
In prescribing prices . . . the board . . . shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations,
-which are accepted by the federation as expressing, as they say, "exactly the objective of organized agriculture in Canada today", are more easily understood than an algebraic formula.
The algebraic formula which was presented to us is based on the years 1925-29. Ours is based on the years 1943-45, and the general

Supply-Agriculture
opinion of experts is that our years are more favourable to the farmer. But I am pleased to note that their formula proves our board to have arrived at about the same support price as the proposed formula would have produced, except that one would not be able to prove at which point between 65 per cent and 85 per cent of parity one should stop. The federation disagrees with the hon. member for Assiniboia when he advocates 100 per cent of parity. They say there should not be an incentive price. We agree. They ask that the support price be between 65 per cent and 85 per cent of parity.
No matter what formula one follows, living as we do alongside a great populous country whose products could flood our country if our prices were higher than theirs, one's last act must be to check their prices and bring ours into proper relationship with theirs.
The formula would produce 23-7 cents as half way between 65 and 85 per cent of parity for hogs. Our support is 23 cents. So we are only a decimal of one cent out from what their algebraic formula would produce.
The formula would produce 59-7 cents as 85 per cent of parity for butter. That is what they would set as the top level. There is a 12-cent duty on butter. Our support price is 58 cents. The U.S.A. support is lower and American butter does not come in because of the duty.
The formula would produce 25 cents as 70 per cent of parity for cheese. Our guarantee has been 24 cents and our support plus the Ontario government's support works out at 80 per cent of parity.
The plan we follow on eggs does not lend itself to the same check but the average price received for eggs since the plan was established five years ago is within the 65 to 85 per cent of parity range.
It is not suggested by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture that we should cover beef or cattle with a support price but the table shows 85 per cent of parity to be $19.60 a hundred for good steers at Toronto. That is the price we are getting and seems to support our practice of allowing the United States market to provide the support for cattle. That is the reason, of course, that the federation does not ask for a support price on cattle.
We are more than pleased to find, now that the federation has worked out a formula, it verifies the supports we have as being reasonable and meeting as nearly as can be the wishes of the organized farmer.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture represents farm organizations in all the provinces of Canada. I am quoting from them rather than from the farmers' union, because
{Mr. Gardiner.]
the farmers' union has not yet established itself right across Canada. Their organization is strong in the three prairie provinces and is attempting to work its way into other provinces, but the federation is organized right across Canada. Their annual convention and submission to the government is most helpful in keeping us in touch with the point of view of the farmer. Even when we are not able to put into effect all the suggestions they make, a discussion brings out ideas which are certain to find their way into administrative activities.
No sound conclusion can be reached by comparing anything related to production or returns from farming, by comparing one year with the one before it or the one immediately after it. Take last year, for example, and compare the wheat production or the final returns with the year before, and the only sound conclusion you can arrive at is that there was a wheat crop failure on account of rust over a considerable area. But if one takes the average over three or four years and compares it with the average over any other three or four years, one can conclude whether prices, income or production are constantly on the upgrade.
I have before me a table which shows that, taking the average price on farm products for the four years before we came into office as the beginning, there has been an increase every four years since, until now the price on all cereals is from 24 to 3 times as high from 1951 to 1954 as in 1931 to 1934. The price on hogs is over three times as high, and the price on cattle over four times as high. The price on butter is 24 times as high, the price on cheese three times as high and the price on eggs almost twice as high.

Even if the dollar were only worth half as much, the returns would be greatly increased.
It is not remarkable that prices went up during the war, but it is remarkable that they have gone up a great deal more since the war than either before or during the war. Cereals have been 75 per cent higher; hogs, steers and butter have brought almost twice as much; and cheese and eggs 50 per cent more during the past four years than during the last four years of the war. This is remarkable as it is eight years since the end of the war. I doubt if there ever was an eight-year period after any previous war when prices for farm products continued higher than during the war. It is partly due
to the fact that we have been spending ten times as much promoting production and marketing in agriculture for many years as was ever spent for that purpose before this government came into office.
But our critics say the cash returns are up but what about the net income. If you average the last four years of net income with any other similar length of period, the results are higher net income in the last four years. The last four years for which I have the net farm income are 1951, 1952, 1953 and 1954. The average net return per year in that period is $1,726 million. The average net return per year for the previous four years is $1,484 million, which is higher than any previous four years. Of course, it is down for

Supply-Agriculture
1954 because of our wheat crop failure and filled elevators, but even the net income for 1954 averaged with the preceding three years is higher than the average of any preceding four-year period. What has kept it that way?
We passed the Agricultural Products Cooperative Marketing Act in 1939. It makes it possible for any group of farmers to organize a pool to sell their product. The federal government guarantees them at the bank so that they can secure sufficient credit to be able to make an advance payment, sell the product, and make a final payment. One hundred and twenty co-operatives have been set up under this legislation which assists in stabilizing returns and returning the highest possible prices to the farmer. The last to be so organized is the cheese board in Ontario.
We put through legislation in 1943 which set up the wheat board in its present form. The wheat board has marketed our wheat in a very satisfactory manner since, with the result that for the first time in our experience surpluses have not driven the price down to the extent that profits could not be made.
We put through the Agricultural Prices Support Act in 1944 and it has operated since 1946. The board set up under it sets up agencies which offer to take delivery of surpluses at floor prices and put them back on the market in times of shortage. The board has a revolving fund of $200 million with which to operate which is kept at that level by amounts from the treasury. They have used $300 million over the nine years, and, with the exception of $70 million spent fighting foot-and-mouth disease, there has been very little which has not been returned to the fund.
Has the minister the exact amount which has not been returned?

The exact amount is the difference between that amount and the $70 million taken off and about another $12 million on top of that $70 million. That is what has not been returned.
Activities under these acts for the past ten years have maintained and stabilized prices on wheat, livestock, potatoes, apples, beans, honey, dry skimmed milk, Cheddar cheese, creamery butter and shell eggs at higher levels than ever before. It is the fact that these prices being kept in reasonable relationship to the prices of what farmers buy has resulted in the average net income of farmers being higher in the last four years than in any previous four-year period.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On Monday we shall take third reading of Bill No. 352 with respect to meat and meat products; second reading of Bill No. 411 with respect to national standards for agricultural products; second reading of Bill No. 5, to amend the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act; and second reading of Bill No. 410, to amend the Customs Act. On conclusion of that business we shall move to go into supply. If we achieve that end we shall continue with Department of Agriculture estimates for the rest of the day.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I would point out that during the current session a committee has been discussing the revision of the rules. It is well known to everyone that in discussing this matter the committee has recognized a long-established practice that the motion to go into supply shall be the first order called on a designated day; and the proposed rules contemplate fixed days for a certain number of motions for going into supply. This is merely expressing a long-established tradition with regard to a practice of long standing, that the motion to go into supply at this stage of the proceedings affords the opportunity for certain stated motions.
One of the things that, it seems to me, should be recognized in this house is the desirability of dates being fixed so that members may make their own arrangements accordingly. Ministers and members find it necessary to be out of the house on various occasions and it should be possible for them to make those arrangements with recognition of important matters coming before the house. One of those important matters is a motion going into supply. I submit that it is simply a breach of a long-established practice to adopt a course like this. It is a practice which means that the motion going into supply is left hanging in suspense. No one knows when it will come up. I repeat the term I used earlier, namely that to adopt this practice is juggling with the traditions of this house and that at a time when an effort is being made to introduce rules which will be satisfactory to everyone.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, those of us who are serving on the rules committee are, of course, obliged not to discuss the matter until a report is made to the house. I take it that that obligation does not devolve upon any hon. members who are not members of the committee.
You told the press what was going on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Under these circumstances I would not comment on what has been said except to say this. I too for a number of years have been trying to get an orderly system of dealing with the business of the house. In the course of the past two years, having had something to do with it, I have done what I could by arrangement with other parties to see if we could not have, as far as possible, an understanding as to the sequence of business so that it would meet the very point the Leader of the Opposition has made. I do not recall at any time it having been said that if the committee were to make the report that the Leader of the Opposition suggests it may be making, it is as a consequence of recognizing a tradition of the house. I do not recall that ever having been said at all in the committee or in the house. While I would be willing to meet any reasonable request, and I have done so over the past two years, I feel that for Monday at least we shall have to go on with the business I have indicated. It may well happen, if the legislation is out of the way, that the motion to go into supply will be the first order of business on Tuesday. I would hope it would be that way.

On a question of privilege, I would point out that it is perfectly proper to discuss something that has already been fully discussed in the press and mainly on information given to the press by the minister himself.
